title: Francesco Sassetti (1421–1490) and His Son Teodoro

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Jules Bache Collection, 1949
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A portrait of an older man and a young boy shown together. The man faces the viewer, while the boy is shown in side view, in profile.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: A tempera painting by the Florentine artist Domenico Ghirlandaio, made around 1488. It shows the banker Francesco Sassetti with his young son Teodoro, who was born in 1479. The Met notes that the father's face was damaged by harsh cleaning long ago and is now largely overpainted.

descriptions.k: A father and his little son are in this picture. The boy is looking to the side. The father looks right at you. They are close together. How do you think they feel about each other?
descriptions.g12: Long ago in Florence, Italy, a rich banker had this picture painted. It shows Francesco Sassetti and his young son Teodoro. The boy is turned to the side, but his father looks out at us. Why do you think the painter showed a father and son together?
descriptions.g35: Domenico Ghirlandaio painted this double portrait in Florence, Italy, around 1488. Francesco Sassetti was a banker who managed branches of the Medici bank, and Teodoro was his young son, born in 1479. The boy is shown in profile, while his father faces us with a thoughtful look. Compare the two faces. What do the different poses tell you about each person?
descriptions.g68: Ghirlandaio painted this in tempera, an egg-based paint, around 1488. Francesco Sassetti managed Medici banks in several cities, and the picture shows him with his son Teodoro, born in 1479. The Met calls it a dynastic portrait: it presents a family and its future. The boy is in profile, a convention linked with purity and youth, while his father's direct, contemplative gaze suggests the cares of age. What might each pose communicate? How do the two figures relate?
descriptions.g910: This double portrait of about 1488 presents a Florentine banker and his heir as a statement about family continuity. Ghirlandaio contrasts the father's frontal, contemplative gaze with the boy's profile, a pose associated with innocence and, in the Met's reading, with the holiness linked to women and children. Teodoro was named for an elder brother who died the year he was born, which may add poignancy for modern viewers. Tempera's clarity suits the careful, almost sculptural modeling of faces. Note too that the father's face was heavily overpainted after damage.
descriptions.g1112: Ghirlandaio's portrait of Francesco Sassetti and Teodoro works as a dynastic image: wealth, lineage, and hope for the next generation are condensed into two faces. The father's frontal gaze and the boy's profile set up a contrast of experience and youth that scholars link to Renaissance conventions of portraiture. We should be cautious, however: the father's face was obliterated by harsh cleaning before 1894 and is largely overpainted, so what we read as his expression is partly a later hand. How should that change the way we describe the picture's emotional effect?

k.daily: The father looks at you, and the boy looks away. What do you think the boy is looking at?
k.emotion: Do these two look happy, serious, or quiet? What makes you think so?
k.observation: Find the man and the boy. What is the same about them, and what is different?
k.analysis: Which face do you look at first, the man or the boy? Why?
k.line: Trace the side of the boy's face from his forehead to his chin with your finger in the air.
k.shape: What shapes do you see in the faces and the hair?
k.color: Which colors do you see around the two faces? Which one stands out most?
k.texture: How would the boy's hair feel to touch? Soft, curly, or smooth?
k.space: Who is closer to you, the man or the boy? How can you tell?
k.light: Where is the light on their faces? Which parts are darker?
k.meaning: What do you think the father hopes for his son? Tell your idea.
k.culture: This was painted in Italy a very long time ago. What is different from a photo of a family today?
k.technique: This painting was made with paint that has egg in it. What else could an artist use to paint?
k.personal: Who do you like to spend time with? Tell about a picture of you with them.
k.critical: Why might someone have a painting made of their family instead of a photo?

g12.daily: How are the father and the boy shown differently? What does each pose make you think?
g12.emotion: What feeling do you get from the two faces? Which part of the picture helps you feel that way?
g12.observation: Describe three details about the man and three about the boy.
g12.analysis: How does the artist show that these two people belong together?
g12.line: Follow the outline of the boy's face in profile. Is it soft or sharp? How does that change the feeling?
g12.shape: Look at the two heads. How do their sizes and shapes fit together in the picture?
g12.color: Which colors are bright and which are quiet? How do they help you notice the faces?
g12.texture: Which things in the picture look smooth and which look soft? Show how you can tell.
g12.space: How does the artist show who is in front and who is behind?
g12.light: Where does the light fall on the faces? What does it help you see?
g12.meaning: Why might a father want a portrait with his son in it? What could it say about their family?
g12.culture: The father was a banker in Florence, Italy. What might a picture like this tell people about him?
g12.technique: Ghirlandaio used tempera paint on wood. How might a wooden panel be different from paper?
g12.personal: If you had a portrait with someone in your family, who would it be and why?
g12.critical: The boy is seen from the side and the man looks at us. Why might a painter choose two different poses?

g35.daily: Look at the two faces. What can you tell about the father and son from how they are shown?
g35.emotion: What mood does the portrait create? Which details make you feel that way?
g35.observation: Take one minute of silent looking. What small details about faces, hair, or clothing do you notice?
g35.analysis: How does Ghirlandaio use the father's direct gaze and the boy's side view to organize the portrait?
g35.line: How do the clear outlines of the faces help you see each person?
g35.shape: How do the shapes of the two heads work together? Which one seems bigger and why?
g35.color: How do the colors help you notice the faces first? What would happen if the colors were duller?
g35.texture: How does the painter make skin and hair look different from each other?
g35.space: The two people are close together and close to us. How does that make you feel as a viewer?
g35.light: How does the light shape the faces and make them look rounded?
g35.meaning: The Met calls this a dynastic portrait, one about a family's future. What details might suggest that?
g35.culture: Sassetti was a banker working with the powerful Medici family in Renaissance Florence. Why might wealthy families order portraits?
g35.technique: Tempera is made with egg and dries fast. Why might a painter work in small, careful strokes with it?
g35.personal: How would you like your family to be remembered in a picture? What would you include?
g35.critical: How do you think we can know what the people in old portraits were really like? What might we guess wrong?

g68.daily: What does the contrast between the father's frontal gaze and the boy's profile suggest about their relationship?
g68.emotion: Is the mood serious, tender, or something else? Use evidence from the faces and poses.
g68.observation: Describe the two figures without interpreting. Which details seem most carefully painted?
g68.analysis: How does the composition tie the two figures together while keeping each one distinct?
g68.line: How do the strong outlines of the profile and the softer lines of the father's face create contrast?
g68.shape: How do the sizes and positions of the two heads create a sense of generations?
g68.color: How does the palette keep attention on the faces? What roles do the darker and lighter areas play?
g68.texture: How does tempera, with its fine lines of paint, shape the way hair and skin look here?
g68.space: How close does the picture place us to these two people? How does that affect our feeling about them?
g68.light: How does the even, clear light help show form without strong shadows?
g68.meaning: Teodoro was named after an older brother who died the year he was born. How might knowing that change how you look at the portrait?
g68.culture: How did Renaissance Florence's bankers and merchants use art to show family pride and status?
g68.technique: Why might a damaged and overpainted face matter when we read a portrait's expression?
g68.personal: How do the portraits you see of families today show pride, memory, or hope? How are they similar or different?
g68.critical: The father's face has been repaired and overpainted. How should that affect what we say about the painting?

g910.daily: How does the pairing of frontal father and profile son construct a story about generations without any action?
g910.emotion: How do restrained expression and close placement produce emotion in this double portrait?
g910.observation: Describe the visual hierarchy of the portrait. What draws attention first, and how do the poses direct it?
g910.analysis: Analyze how Ghirlandaio balances individual likeness with the portrait's role as a family statement.
g910.line: How does the crisp profile contour of the boy function differently from the more modeled treatment of the father?
g910.shape: How do the two heads, different in scale and angle, create a rhythm across the panel?
g910.color: How does the painter use color and tone to unify two figures while keeping each distinct?
g910.texture: How does tempera's clarity influence the rendering of hair, skin, and fabric compared with softer oil techniques?
g910.space: How does the shallow, close-up space create intimacy and also formality?
g910.light: How does the even illumination support the portrait's clear, sculptural treatment of form?
g910.meaning: How might the profile pose, associated with purity and youth, shape the viewer's response to Teodoro?
g910.culture: How did Florentine banking families such as the Sassetti use portraits to express lineage and status?
g910.technique: What does it mean to study a portrait whose central face has been heavily overpainted? What can still be trusted?
g910.personal: How do you think representations of family in your own life shape how you read this one?
g910.critical: How might a portrait made to honor a family also hide aspects of the sitters? What evidence would you want?

g1112.daily: What can be argued about this portrait's purpose from the poses of father and son, and what remains uncertain?
g1112.emotion: How can a portrait convey feeling when conventions of pose limit expression? Where do you see emotion, and could it come from restoration?
g1112.observation: Describe the portrait's construction precisely. Which observations depend on areas that have been overpainted?
g1112.analysis: Analyze how the portrait balances individuality and convention, including the use of profile and frontal poses.
g1112.line: How does the use of contour for the boy and modeling for the man signal different ways of describing a person?
g1112.shape: How does the interplay of the two heads, one frontal and one in profile, structure the panel?
g1112.color: How should we weigh the influence of cleaning and overpainting when we discuss the portrait's color and tone?
g1112.texture: How does tempera's linear, layered handling shape the illusion of hair and skin, and what does that say about Florentine taste?
g1112.space: How does the near, shallow space shape the viewer's relationship with the sitters?
g1112.light: In what ways does consistent, even light serve the portrait's aims, compared with the dramatic light of later portraiture?
g1112.meaning: Evaluate the idea that this is a dynastic portrait. What does the image support, and what depends on historical knowledge outside the picture?
g1112.culture: How do banking networks like the Medici's help explain the commissioning of portraits like this one?
g1112.technique: How does the history of damage and restoration complicate claims about the artist's intention and skill?
g1112.personal: What assumptions about childhood and family do you bring to this image? How might a Renaissance viewer have differed?
g1112.critical: How should museums communicate the effect of past restoration to viewers who expect to see an artist's original hand?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Subject, title, classification, and tags (Boys, Men, Portraits) checked against the museum record.

teacherNote.context: A double portrait painted in Florence around 1488. The Met describes it as a dynastic portrait and notes that the father's face was damaged by harsh cleaning before 1894 and is now overpainted.
directions: Have students sketch the boy in profile and the man in frontal view, then discuss what each pose communicates.
Ask students to design a portrait showing their family that tells viewers something about its values.
Discuss how a painting can change over time because of damage and repair.
